name: Tails
purpose: Live operating system booted from a USB stick that routes all network traffic through Tor, leaves no trace on the host computer by default, and bundles encryption, secure deletion and anonymity tooling.
journalism_use_case: The standard tool for working on sensitive material on a machine you do not trust, or for a source who must contact you without leaving evidence on their own computer: boot Tails, work, shut down, and the computer retains nothing. Also the historical environment for handling the most sensitive leaks.
pros: Amnesia by default is a structural protection no application can provide: nothing written to the host disk means nothing to find in a later device search
All traffic forced through Tor removes the commonest operational-security mistake — a single application leaking outside the tunnel
Actively maintained with a visible release cadence (Tails 7.17 announced on the project's news page, verified 2026-11-17) and a long institutional track record in press-freedom contexts
Optional encrypted persistent storage lets a journalist keep keys and documents across sessions when amnesia is inconvenient, as an explicit choice
cons: Developed on the project's own GitLab rather than GitHub, so it is invisible to GitHub-based discovery and dependency tooling; the GitHub path TAILS-Project/TAILS is an unrelated stub (1 star, last push 2017) and must not be mistaken for it
Booting from USB requires access to firmware settings, which managed, corporate or locked-down laptops often prevent — and in some countries carrying a Tails USB is itself incriminating
Tor-only networking is slow and breaks many ordinary web services, so it is a dedicated-session tool rather than a daily environment
Persistent storage, if enabled, reintroduces exactly the forensic trace that amnesia removes — a configuration choice with serious consequences that users make casually
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: Tails 7.17 is the most recent release announced on tails.net/news (retrieved 2026-11-17), and the project's own GitLab instance is the development home — the GitLab API on that host is not publicly queryable, so maintenance was verified from the release announcements instead. Tails's role in high-profile leak handling is extensively documented publicly.
assessment: Adopt as a standard capability: keep prepared Tails USB sticks and train reporters to use them for first contact with unknown material and for work on untrusted machines. For your profile, two points matter particularly in exile contexts. First, possession can be a risk in itself — think about where sticks are stored and how they look. Second, decide a policy on persistence: amnesia is the protection, and a persistent volume full of documents on a USB stick in a journalist's bag is a different and worse threat model than they imagine.
maintenance_evidence: Release announcements on tails.net/news retrieved 2026-11-17 show Tails 7.17 as the current release, with the 7.x line in active development. Development occurs on gitlab.tails.boum.org (API not publicly queryable, so repository-level metrics are unavailable). The unrelated GitHub stub TAILS-Project/TAILS (1 star, pushed 2017-10-20) is NOT the project and should not be cited.
licence: GPL-3.0-or-later (project licensing; the distribution aggregates many components under their own licences)
model_or_data_licence: n/a. The distribution bundles software under many licences.
licence_restrictions: Aggregate free-software licensing; immaterial for use. Redistribution of a modified Tails image would require attention to the component licences.
costs: No fee. A USB stick per user (negligible) plus the time to prepare and verify images. Verification of the download signature is an essential, non-optional step and takes a few minutes.
privacy: The strongest privacy posture available in a general-purpose environment: no host disk writes, all traffic over Tor, memory wiped on shutdown. Residual risks are physical (possession of the stick), firmware-level compromise of the host, and user error in enabling persistence.
alternatives: Qubes OS for a compartmentalised daily-use system rather than an amnesic session
A dedicated air-gapped laptop for the most sensitive material
Whonix for Tor-routed virtual machines on an existing host
blockers: Requires firmware access to boot from USB; possession may itself carry risk in hostile jurisdictions
summary: Live operating system booted from a USB stick that routes all network traffic through Tor…
additional_costs_note: staff time to prepare and verify images; a USB stick per user (negligible)

name: Qubes OS
purpose: Security-focused desktop operating system that runs applications in isolated Xen-based virtual machines organised by trust level, with disposable VMs, a separate networking VM and controlled inter-VM file transfer.
journalism_use_case: A daily-use environment where compromise is contained: open an untrusted attachment in a disposable VM that is destroyed afterwards, keep source communications in one compartment and ordinary browsing in another, so a malicious document or a phishing click cannot reach your notes or your keys.
pros: Compartmentalisation is the only architecture here that assumes compromise will happen and limits what it reaches — the right model for a journalist who must open attachments from strangers
Disposable VMs make opening an untrusted document safe by construction, which is Dangerzone's protection generalised to everything
Underpins SecureDrop Workstation, so adopting Qubes brings the recommended submission-handling workflow within reach
Long-standing project with institutional respect in the security community and a documented release and security-advisory process
cons: Hardware compatibility is genuinely restrictive: Qubes needs specific virtualisation and IOMMU support, and the certified-hardware list is short — procurement is the first obstacle and in some regions a decisive one
Steep learning curve and real daily friction: moving files between compartments is deliberate work, and users who find it tedious will subvert it

The GitHub presence is an issue tracker (QubesOS/qubes-issues, no releases, no detected licence), so repository metadata tells you nothing about the OS's health — assessment must come from the project's own release and advisory channels
Resource-hungry: comfortable use needs substantial RAM and a fast SSD, so older laptops are unusable
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: the GitHub repository QubesOS/qubes-issues is a tracker (624 stars, no releases, last push 2026-07-08, no detected licence) rather than the OS source, so maintenance was not assessed from it. Qubes's adoption in high-threat journalism and its use as the basis of SecureDrop Workstation are documented by FPF.
assessment: Adopt for the people who most need it — reporters handling unsolicited material and anyone working on a high-risk investigation — provided you can procure certified hardware and support the learning curve. For your profile the realistic path is a small number of Qubes machines for specific roles rather than an organisation-wide rollout, paired with SecureDrop Workstation if you run a submission system. Where Qubes is impractical, Tails for sessions plus Dangerzone for documents covers much of the same risk at far lower cost.
maintenance_evidence: Assessed from the project's own release and security-advisory process rather than GitHub, since QubesOS/qubes-issues is only a tracker (no releases, pushed 2026-07-08, no detected licence). The project maintains a published advisory stream and a certified-hardware programme; this classification is therefore medium-confidence on evidence type, not on the conclusion.
licence: GPL-2.0 (project licensing; the distribution aggregates components under their own licences)
licence_restrictions: Aggregate free-software licensing; immaterial for use.
costs: No software fee. Certified hardware is the cost: a Qubes-capable laptop with substantial RAM and SSD (estimate: mid-to-upper four figures for a small team), plus training and support time. The hardware constraint is the real budget item.
privacy: Compartmentalisation limits what a compromise reaches, and the networking VM isolates the network stack. It is not an anonymity system — Qubes protects against compromise, Tails protects against tracing, and they answer different questions. Whonix VMs inside Qubes combine both.
alternatives: Tails for amnesic, Tor-routed sessions rather than daily compartmentalisation
Dangerzone plus a hardened conventional OS as a much cheaper partial mitigation
A dedicated, network-isolated laptop for the highest-risk material
blockers: Restrictive certified-hardware requirement; substantial learning curve and resource needs
summary: Security-focused desktop operating system that runs applications in isolated Xen-based virtual machines organised by trust level…
additional_costs_note: dedicated hardware; self-hosted infrastructure; staff effort

name: security-misc (Kicksecure)
purpose: Package of Linux security-hardening settings — kernel parameters, module blacklists, access restrictions, boot and memory protections — applied as a coherent set rather than individually.
journalism_use_case: Hardening the Linux machines a newsroom actually runs — the document-processing workstation, the evidence machine, the server holding an archive — using settings maintained by a security-focused distribution rather than assembling kernel flags from blog posts.
pros: Provides a curated, maintained hardening baseline, which is substantially better than the ad-hoc hardening most organisations attempt and then never revisit
Developed for Kicksecure and Whonix, so the settings come from a project whose purpose is a hardened system rather than from general-purpose advice
Modular enough to apply selectively, and documented so you can understand what each setting costs in functionality
Active maintenance (pushed 2026-09-30, tag 54.2-1) with a focused community (600 stars)
cons: Hardening breaks things: module blacklists and restrictive kernel parameters can disable hardware or software you need, and diagnosing the cause afterwards is unpleasant — test before deploying to a working machine
No release objects (tag-based versioning only) and GitHub reports no SPDX licence, so the licence must be read from the repository for compliance records
Debian-family oriented, so applying it to other distributions requires adaptation
Hardening is not a substitute for architecture: a hardened machine that still opens untrusted documents directly is less safe than an unhardened one using Dangerzone or disposable VMs
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 600 stars with 36 open issues, no releases, latest tag 54.2-1, last push 2026-09-30, no SPDX detected. Its use as a component of Kicksecure and Whonix is documented by those projects, which is the relevant production context.
assessment: Worth applying to your infrastructure machines, with testing — and worth understanding as the second line of defence rather than the first. For your profile the priority order matters: compartmentalisation and document sanitisation (Qubes, Tails, Dangerzone) prevent whole classes of attack, while hardening reduces the damage of what gets through. Apply it to the archive server and the evidence workstation, test thoroughly, and document which settings you disabled and why.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-09-30, no release objects, latest tag 54.2-1, no SPDX detected, 600 stars, 36 open issues. Regular tag-based versioning with current commits as a component of an actively maintained distribution.
licence: Not detected by the GitHub API — read the repository licence file before redistribution (the Kicksecure/Whonix ecosystem is predominantly GPL-family)
licence_restrictions: Unverified in this survey; confirm from the repository before including it in a distributed image.
costs: No fee. Cost is testing and troubleshooting time, which is non-trivial on diverse hardware.
privacy: Local system configuration; no data flows. Note that some settings reduce telemetry and network exposure, which is a privacy improvement in itself.
alternatives: Distribution-provided hardening guides (Debian, Ubuntu security guides) for a more conservative baseline
Qubes OS, which addresses the same risk architecturally rather than by configuration
CIS benchmarks for a formal, auditable hardening standard
summary: Package of Linux security-hardening settings — kernel parameters, module blacklists, access restrictions…

name: VeraCrypt
purpose: Disk-encryption software creating encrypted containers and full-disk encryption on Windows, macOS and Linux, with hidden volumes and plausible-deniability features, derived from TrueCrypt.
journalism_use_case: Encrypting the archive of source material that must travel or be stored outside a controlled environment — an external drive carried across a border, a backup held off-site, or a container holding a leak on a shared workstation. The hidden-volume feature is sometimes used in high-risk travel, with serious caveats.
pros: Cross-platform encrypted containers are the practical answer for material that must move between operating systems, where platform-native encryption (BitLocker, FileVault, LUKS) does not interoperate
Full-disk and container modes cover both the laptop and the external drive cases with one tool and one mental model
Actively maintained (VeraCrypt_1.26.31, 2026-11-02; pushed 2026-11-16) with a large user base (12,148 stars) and a TrueCrypt lineage that has been independently audited over the years
Open source, so the encryption implementation can be examined rather than trusted on vendor assurance
cons: Hidden volumes provide plausible deniability only in theory: under coercive questioning at a border, the existence of VeraCrypt plus a refusal to produce a second password can itself be the problem, and several jurisdictions can compel disclosure — do not present this feature to journalists as safety
GitHub reports SPDX NOASSERTION; the project is licensed under the Apache-2.0 plus TrueCrypt Licence 3.0 combination, which is unusual and needs reading before redistribution
515 open issues and a complex codebase with a single principal maintainer — a notable bus factor for security-critical software
Full-disk encryption on a machine that is seized while running or suspended offers much less protection than users assume
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 12,148 stars with 515 open issues, release VeraCrypt_1.26.31 (2026-11-02), pushed 2026-11-16, SPDX NOASSERTION (the project's licensing combines Apache-2.0 with the TrueCrypt Licence 3.0 for inherited code). VeraCrypt and its TrueCrypt ancestor have been the subject of published independent audits, which is the strongest assurance signal available for encryption software here.
assessment: Adopt for cross-platform encrypted containers, and be careful about how you present it. Two messages for the people you support: encryption protects data at rest on a powered-off device and little else, so shut down rather than suspend when crossing a border; and hidden volumes are not a safe answer to coercion, because the threat at a border is a person, not a cryptanalyst. Where the platform permits, native full-disk encryption (LUKS, FileVault) is simpler and better integrated — use VeraCrypt specifically for portable, cross-platform containers.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release VeraCrypt_1.26.31 (2026-11-02), 12,148 stars, 515 open issues. Regular releases over many years; the large backlog and single-principal-maintainer structure are the notable risks, not activity.
licence: Apache-2.0 plus TrueCrypt Licence 3.0 for inherited code (GitHub reports NOASSERTION)
licence_restrictions: The TrueCrypt Licence 3.0 component is not an OSI-approved licence and has known redistribution ambiguities — relevant if you bundle VeraCrypt into a distributed product or image, immaterial for ordinary use.
costs: No fee. No infrastructure. Cost is user training and the discipline of key management — a forgotten passphrase on an encrypted archive is a permanent data loss.
privacy: Strong at-rest protection when used correctly on a powered-off device. Residual risks are the ones that actually occur: suspended machines, keys in memory, coerced disclosure, and passphrases written down or reused.
alternatives: LUKS (Linux), FileVault (macOS) or BitLocker (Windows) for native full-disk encryption where cross-platform portability is not needed
age or GPG for encrypting individual files for transfer
Tails with an encrypted persistent volume for a portable working environment
blockers: Hidden-volume plausible deniability should not be relied on against coercive questioning
summary: Disk-encryption software creating encrypted containers and full-disk encryption on Windows, macOS and Linux…

name: Signal (Android client)
purpose: End-to-end encrypted messaging application for text, voice and video, with disappearing messages, sealed sender, safety numbers for key verification and encrypted group messaging.
journalism_use_case: The default channel for source communication where a phone number is acceptable: messages and calls are end-to-end encrypted, disappearing messages limit what a seized device reveals, and the protocol is the most scrutinised in the field. In practice it is the channel most sources already have.
pros: The most heavily analysed end-to-end encryption protocol in general use, with repeated independent cryptographic review — the strongest assurance basis of any communications tool here
Disappearing messages and remote-deletion materially reduce what a seized or compromised device yields, which is the realistic threat for most journalists
AGPL-3.0 client and server, actively maintained (v8.35.2, 2026-11-09; pushed 2026-11-16), with reproducible-build efforts and a non-profit operator
Ubiquity matters: a protected channel the source already uses beats a better one they will not install
cons: Requires a phone number, which is an identifier the source must reveal to you and to Signal — a real limitation when the source must not be identifiable at all, and the reason SecureDrop exists

Metadata minimisation is strong but not absolute: Signal knows when accounts registered and, to a limited degree, when they connect, and the operator is subject to legal process (its published transparency responses show it holds very little)
Centralised service dependency: if Signal is blocked in a country, sources need censorship circumvention, and that adds operational burden exactly where it is hardest
Safety-number verification is the step that makes end-to-end encryption meaningful against interception, and almost nobody does it — a training rather than a software problem
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 29,652 stars with 491 open issues, release v8.35.2 (2026-11-09), pushed 2026-11-16, AGPL-3.0; the server (signalapp/Signal-Server, AGPL-3.0, pushed 2026-11-16) is also published, which is unusual and supports the privacy claims. The protocol's cryptographic review record is extensively documented in published literature.
assessment: Adopt as the default communication channel and train safety-number verification, because unverified end-to-end encryption protects against the wrong threat. For your profile the phone-number requirement is the decision point: use Signal for ongoing contact with sources whose identity you already know, and SecureDrop or Hush Line for first contact with sources who must stay anonymous. In exile contexts, plan for Signal being blocked — pre-arrange circumvention and a fallback channel before it is needed.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release v8.35.2 (2026-11-09), tag v8.36.2, 29,652 stars, 491 open issues. Frequent releases under a funded non-profit; the server component is separately published and equally current.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0 on client and server. Note that running a modified client against Signal's servers is contrary to the service's terms regardless of the licence — relevant to forks like Molly.
costs: Free to use. No infrastructure. Cost is training time and the operational work of maintaining circumvention where Signal is blocked.
privacy: End-to-end encrypted content with strong metadata minimisation, backed by a published server implementation and a transparency record showing very little retained data. The irreducible disclosure is the phone number, which is an identifier linking source to journalist.
alternatives: SimpleX Chat where no identifier at all can be exchanged
Molly for a hardened Signal-compatible Android client
SecureDrop or Hush Line for anonymous first contact
blockers: Requires a phone number — unsuitable where the source must not be identifiable
summary: End-to-end encrypted messaging application for text, voice and video, with disappearing messages, sealed sender…

name: Molly
purpose: Hardened fork of Signal for Android that adds database encryption at rest with a separate passphrase, automatic locking, memory wiping, and a build free of proprietary Google dependencies.
journalism_use_case: Signal for a journalist whose device may be seized: Molly encrypts the local message database behind a passphrase and locks automatically, so a seized or borrowed phone does not immediately surrender the message history that standard Signal keeps accessible once the device is unlocked.
pros: Addresses the specific gap that matters most in device seizure: standard Signal's local database is protected only by device encryption, so an unlocked phone exposes the history, while Molly requires a separate passphrase
A Google-free build (Molly-FOSS) matters for de-Googled and GrapheneOS devices, which is the configuration many high-risk journalists use
AGPL-3.0, actively maintained (pushed 2026-11-16) with a substantial community (3,838 stars) and builds tracking upstream Signal releases
Keeps Signal protocol compatibility, so contacts need not change anything
cons: A third-party fork of a security-critical application: you are trusting the Molly maintainers' build and patches in addition to Signal's, which is a genuine supply-chain consideration for the most sensitive use
Running a modified client against Signal's servers is contrary to the service's terms, so there is a (small, historically untested) risk of access disruption
Release cadence trails upstream Signal (v8.19.2-4 from 2026-07-31 against Signal's November release), meaning a period without upstream security fixes after each Signal update
Android only; iOS users have no equivalent, so a mixed-device team cannot standardise on it
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 3,838 stars, release v8.19.2-4 (2026-07-31), pushed 2026-11-16, AGPL-3.0. The release-version gap against upstream Signal (8.19 versus 8.35) is visible in the API data and is the key operational caveat.
assessment: Recommend it selectively — for journalists at genuine risk of device seizure, on Android, who will manage a second passphrase. The at-rest protection is a real improvement over standard Signal for that threat. But the trailing release cadence is a serious counter-consideration: a fork that is sixteen minor versions behind upstream may lack recent security fixes, so check the current gap before deploying and re-check periodically. For most users, standard Signal plus disappearing messages plus strong device encryption is the better trade.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release v8.19.2-4 (2026-07-31), 3,838 stars, AGPL-3.0. Commits are current but the published release trails upstream Signal (v8.35.2) by a substantial margin — activity is clear, release timeliness is the concern.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0. Separately, Signal's terms of service address use of modified clients against its servers — a service-terms rather than licence question.
costs: Free. No infrastructure. Cost is the user managing an additional passphrase and the administrator tracking the upstream version gap.
privacy: Improves on Signal specifically at rest (encrypted local database, auto-lock, memory wiping). In transit it is Signal, with the same phone-number disclosure. The Google-free build removes a dependency on proprietary services.
alternatives: Standard Signal with disappearing messages and strong device encryption for most users
SimpleX Chat where identifier-free contact is the requirement
GrapheneOS plus standard Signal for a hardened device rather than a hardened client
blockers: Release cadence trails upstream Signal — verify the current version gap before deploying
summary: Hardened fork of Signal for Android that adds database encryption at rest with a separate passphrase, automatic locking…

name: SimpleX Chat
purpose: Messaging network with no user identifiers of any kind: contacts connect via one-time invitation links through relay servers that hold no account records, with end-to-end encryption and optional self-hosted relays.
journalism_use_case: First contact with a source who must not reveal a phone number, email address or any persistent identifier — the gap Signal cannot fill. A reporter publishes a one-time invitation link, the source connects, and no account exists on either side to be subpoenaed or correlated.
pros: No user identifiers at all is a genuinely different architecture, not a privacy feature bolted on — there is no account, no phone number and no username to correlate or compel
Self-hostable relays mean a newsroom can run its own infrastructure, so even relay metadata stays within your control
AGPL-3.0 and very actively maintained (v7.1.4, 2026-11-14; pushed 2026-11-17) with a large community (19,711 stars)
Fills the specific operational gap between anonymous submission systems and identified messaging, which nothing else here covers well
cons: 1,333 open issues — the largest backlog of any communications tool here — reflecting a young, fast-moving project; security-critical software with that profile warrants caution for the highest-risk use
Far less independent cryptographic review than Signal, which is the decisive consideration when the threat is a state adversary — novel architecture means novel risk
Usability is weaker than Signal: invitation-link exchange is unfamiliar, and because there are no accounts, losing the app or device can mean losing contacts irrecoverably
A source must install an app nobody has heard of, which is itself a barrier and, in a hostile environment, a conspicuous artefact on their device
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 19,711 stars with 1,333 open issues, release v7.1.4 (2026-11-14), pushed 2026-11-17, AGPL-3.0. The identifier-free design is documented by the project; the volume of open issues relative to other messengers here is the notable signal and is visible in the API data.
assessment: Pilot it for the identifier-free first-contact case, where it does something nothing else does — but do not displace Signal for ongoing source communication, because Signal's review record matters more than SimpleX's architectural elegance when the adversary is capable. For your profile the sensible posture is: publish a SimpleX invitation alongside your SecureDrop or Hush Line address as an alternative for sources who want live conversation without an identifier, self-host the relay, and keep Signal as the workhorse.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v7.1.4 (2026-11-14), 19,711 stars, 1,333 open issues. Same-day commits and a rapid release cadence; the large backlog indicates a project moving faster than it can close issues, which is a maturity caveat rather than a neglect signal.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0: a modified self-hosted relay offered to users obliges source publication.
costs: Free to use. Self-hosting relays: a small VM each — low cost and worth it for metadata control. Estimate.
privacy: Architecturally the strongest metadata position of any messenger here: no identifiers, no accounts, and relays that hold no user records; self-hosting removes even relay-operator visibility. The counterweight is maturity — less reviewed code in a source-protection path is itself a risk.
alternatives: Signal for a reviewed, ubiquitous channel where a phone number is acceptable
SecureDrop for anonymous document submission rather than conversation
Briar for peer-to-peer messaging over Tor with no servers at all
blockers: Much less independent cryptographic review than Signal; large open-issue backlog for security-critical software
summary: Messaging network with no user identifiers of any kind: contacts connect via one-time invitation links through relay servers…

name: Delta Chat / chatmail core
purpose: Rust core library behind Delta Chat, providing end-to-end encrypted messaging over ordinary email infrastructure (SMTP/IMAP) with automatic Autocrypt-style key exchange, plus support for dedicated low-metadata 'chatmail' servers.
journalism_use_case: Encrypted messaging that travels over email, so it works wherever email works — including networks that block Signal and SimpleX. For a source in a country where messaging apps are blocked but email is not, Delta Chat may be the only encrypted channel available.
pros: Using email as transport is the decisive property in censored networks: blocking Delta Chat means blocking email, which states are far more reluctant to do
No new account needed in principle — a source with an email address can participate, lowering the adoption barrier that defeats other tools
Chatmail servers are purpose-built to minimise retained metadata, and the ecosystem is self-hostable, so a newsroom can run its own
Actively maintained (v2.69.0, 2026-11-09; pushed 2026-11-16) with the repository transfer deltachat/deltachat-core-rust → chatmail/core verified by redirect in this session
cons: Email metadata is the weak point: unless both parties use chatmail servers, the message path reveals sender, recipient and timing to mail providers — encryption protects content, not the relationship
Using an existing email address links the conversation to an existing identity, which is the opposite of what anonymous first contact requires
GitHub reports SPDX NOASSERTION, so the licence must be read from the repository (the project is GPL-family) before any redistribution
137 open issues and a complex interaction with diverse mail-server behaviour, so reliability varies by provider in ways that are hard to predict
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 950 stars with 137 open issues, release v2.69.0 (2026-11-09), pushed 2026-11-16, SPDX NOASSERTION; the repository transfer from deltachat/deltachat-core-rust to chatmail/core was confirmed by API redirect on 2026-11-17 and is recorded in leads.md L4. The chatmail server model is documented by the project.
assessment: Keep it in the toolkit specifically as the censorship-resistant option — if Signal and SimpleX are blocked where your sources are, this is what remains. For your profile the configuration that matters is both parties on chatmail servers, which is what removes the mail-metadata problem; Delta Chat over ordinary mailboxes protects content while exposing the relationship, and that distinction must be explained to a source rather than assumed. Update any pinned references to the old deltachat-core-rust path.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release v2.69.0 (2026-11-09), 950 stars, 137 open issues, SPDX NOASSERTION. Frequent releases under the renamed organisation; transfer verified by redirect.
licence: Not detected by the GitHub API — read the repository licence file (the Delta Chat/chatmail ecosystem is GPL-family) before redistribution
licence_restrictions: Unverified in this survey; confirm from the repository before building a product on it.
costs: Free to use. Self-hosting a chatmail server: a small VM plus a mail domain — low cost and the configuration that makes the privacy properties real. Estimate.
privacy: Content is end-to-end encrypted. Metadata depends entirely on the servers: chatmail servers minimise retention, while ordinary mail providers see the sender-recipient relationship and timing. Choose the configuration deliberately and explain it to sources.
alternatives: Signal where it is reachable and a phone number is acceptable
SimpleX Chat for identifier-free contact where it is not blocked
Tor plus any of the above where the network blocks everything
blockers: Mail metadata exposes the sender-recipient relationship unless both parties use chatmail servers
summary: Rust core library behind Delta Chat, providing end-to-end encrypted messaging over ordinary email infrastructure (SMTP/IMAP) with…
